jupyter: python3

The pages in this section compare convinterp with the established alternatives in Python —
SciPy's interpolators and NumPy's Chebyshev interpolation — on the same test functions and
with the same measurements as the [Julia benchmarks](../julia/index.qmd), and every figure and
number is computed from the installed versions when the site is rendered. The scripts are the
code cells themselves, folded on the pages.

## What is compared

| Page | convinterp against |
|:--|:--|
| [Interpolation](interpolation.qmd) | SciPy `CubicSpline`, `make_interp_spline`, NumPy Chebyshev |
| [Derivatives](derivatives.qmd) | SciPy `CubicSpline`, `make_interp_spline`, NumPy Chebyshev |
| [Integration](integration.qmd) | SciPy `CubicSpline`, `make_interp_spline`, `simpson`, `romb` |

The port has the three capabilities above; the pages grow as the port does. The port gives
the same numbers as ConvolutionInterpolations.jl, so for the capabilities not yet ported the
Julia pages show what to expect.

## How

**Accuracy** is the largest absolute error against the exact function on a fine grid of test
points, as a function of the number of samples, on Runge's function $1/(1 + 25x^2)$ on
$[-1, 1]$ — smooth, but with a narrow peak that is the classical difficulty for polynomial
interpolation. Derivatives and integrals are compared with the exact ones of the same
function. Each method is used at its own highest practical order: SciPy's B-spline
interpolant is given degree 7 as well as the cubic, and Chebyshev interpolation — which
chooses its own sample points and so is not an option for data on a grid — is shown as the
reference for what any polynomial method can reach.

**Time** is measured with `timeit`, as the minimum over repeated runs, for construction and
evaluation separately: convinterp computes nothing at construction beyond the boundary values,
and evaluates in constant time per point whatever the grid size, so where the time goes
differs between the packages.

Timings depend on the machine. The ones on these pages were measured on:

- Python 3.12.3, NumPy 2.2.6, SciPy 1.13.0, on Intel64 Family 6 Model 183 Stepping 1, GenuineIntel, 28 threads


Relative timings transfer to other machines better than absolute ones.

## What the comparisons do not show

SciPy's interpolators are mature and general, and the comparisons are on the ground the
convolution kernels were designed for: uniform grids, smooth data, high accuracy. A method
built for other ground — monotone data (`PchipInterpolator`), unstructured points
(`griddata`, `RBFInterpolator`), extrapolation — is not worse for losing a comparison here.

---

*Rendered with Python 3.12.3 on a Intel64 Family 6 Model 183 Stepping 1, GenuineIntel machine (28 threads), with convinterp 0.2.0, numpy 2.2.6, scipy 1.13.0.*
